metadata.title: Why Does a Steel Ship Float?
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: A block of steel sinks in water. So why does a steel ship float?
beats.new_visual_element: Portrait-only opening question card (title-styled, crimson underline).

beats.narration_text: Steel is nearly eight times as dense as water. Drop a solid block of it into a pool, and it sinks straight to the bottom.
beats.new_visual_element: Cross-section of a pool (light-blue water, dark-blue surface line). A grey steel block labeled 'steel' drops in from above and sinks to the floor, a few bubbles rising behind it.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: pool with steel block resting on the floor

beats.narration_text: Yet a ship built from that same steel floats. The material has not changed, so something other than the material must decide whether an object floats or sinks.
beats.new_visual_element: On the right, a grey steel hull with a small mast and crimson flag floats at the surface, labeled 'same steel'.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: sunken block left, floating steel ship right

beats.narration_text: Archimedes' principle states that the buoyant force on an object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces. A submerged block displaces only its own volume of water, and that water weighs about one eighth as much as the steel. The upward push loses, and the block sinks.
beats.new_visual_element: The ship fades. The block is shown fully submerged mid-water with a dashed teal 'displaced water' outline its own size; a long ink arrow W down and a short teal arrow F_B up (about W/8). Equation F_B = w_fl ≈ W/8. The block then sinks back to the floor.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: pool, block, displaced-volume ghost, W and F_B arrows, F_B = w_fl

beats.narration_text: Now reshape the same steel into a hollow hull. Its mass is unchanged, but the hull encloses a far larger volume, so it can push aside much more water before it is submerged.
beats.new_visual_element: The block lifts out of the water and morphs (ReplacementTransform) into a thin-walled hollow hull with the same cross-sectional amount of steel. The hull is lowered onto the water and settles; a large dashed teal displaced-volume region grows beneath the waterline as it sinks in.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: pool, floating hull, large displaced-volume ghost

beats.narration_text: The hull settles until the water it displaces weighs exactly as much as the ship. At that depth the buoyant force balances the weight, and the ship floats. Put another way, the average density of the steel and the air it encloses is less than the density of water.
beats.new_visual_element: Ink arrow W down (same length as the block's) inside the hull and an equally long teal arrow F_B up beneath the hull. Equations F_B = w_fl = W and average density of ship < ρ_water.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: floating hull, ghost volume, equal W and F_B, balance equations

beats.narration_text: Whether an object floats is decided not by what it is made of, but by how much water it can push aside. Same steel, different shape.
beats.new_visual_element: Held frame: the sunken block returns on the floor at left labeled 'sinks', the hull at right labeled 'floats'; summary line 'SAME STEEL, DIFFERENT SHAPE'.
